title: How Duke Books Sells 200,000 Copies of Every Title | The Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic of Duke Books (Part 2)
excerpt: What does this company actually do? In today's book market, it sells an average of more than 200,000 copies per title.
body:
What does this company actually do? In today's book market, it sells an average of more than 200,000 copies per title.

Previously: we set out to introduce a publisher that thinks clearly about publishing and about "how to promote a book as a product." The company, Duke Books, is worth watching.

[As we noted in the previous article](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/14643.html), the success of *Tibet Code* (《藏地密码》) gave Hua Nan great confidence. That confidence did not come from sales alone, since any publisher can turn out a bestseller now and then. It was closer to the joy of an experiment that finally worked after many tries.

The "experiment" was selling books the Duke way: always start from what readers need, make them want to buy by improving how the content is arranged and designed, and take marketing seriously without depending on it.

Some of these lessons came from Hua Nan's earlier career in advertising, but most were learned in Duke's first few years. In other words, the tuition was not cheap.

### "Not a single yuan may be spent marketing any book. To justify the kind of marketing normal for consumer goods, a book would have to sell at least a million copies, and almost none do."

Soon after it was founded, Duke published an urban novel, *Zhao Ganlü's Elevator Adventures* (《赵赶驴电梯奇遇记》). It sold more than 100,000 copies and still lost money, because the company spent too much marketing it. Hua Nan says the lesson was a painful one: "We spent money we couldn't earn back. We made a big noise across the country, book signings and all that, and sales were decent, but when we did the math we had lost money. Later we realized books can't bear that kind of marketing. There's a ceiling. For a book to bear the normal marketing of a consumer product, it would have to sell at least a million copies, and almost no book does that well."

Duke's rule now, Hua Nan says, is "not a single yuan on marketing any book." He found that paid marketing didn't work anyway. "In fact, no book can be made a hit through marketing. The only thing that works is word of mouth."

Word of mouth can be kept up without spending money; what it costs is labor and brainpower. "Our rule for editors is: you can't buy ad placements, and you can't game the rankings. You make content, and you make the content of your posts good." When *Tibet Code* came out, Duke's editors were active on online forums and on the book channels of portals such as Sina Reading. One reader online recalled that more than a thousand reviews of *Tibet Code* appeared on the internet in a single week.

In recent years new media has taken off, which suits Duke, a company that doesn't want to spend money, perfectly. "Duke runs Weibo and WeChat accounts. We've reached the point where I post one message and the Amazon rankings move. That comes from years of building a following. It's all been accumulated over the years, one post at a time."

Besides its own accounts, there are the big marketing accounts. "We work with some accounts. But the company doesn't spend money. Editors do their own math: once a book has sold a certain number of copies, they can (take a bit out of their commission) to have one of those marketing accounts repost something. You pay someone 200 yuan for a repost. If it cost a few thousand, I doubt they'd be willing." Then he came back to brainpower: "It depends on the content. The other day I saw *People's Daily* repost a Duke Weibo post. They did it on their own, and promoted 20 or 30 of our books in one go. Make the content good enough and other people will want to repost it for you."

Duke has just over 70 employees, more than 30 of them in editorial. The entire marketing department is 4 people: 1 for WeChat, 1 for Weibo. "Every one of our departments is the smallest in the business. Motie, Booky and ThinkingDom each have several hundred people. We are the only independent company among the top-tier publishers, with no outside funding at all. We are fairly conservative. ThinkingDom will set up a new department and put ten people in it to start. We wouldn't dare."

Conservative means doing only what is necessary. "'Not a single yuan' is too absolute. Signings and launch events cost money, and engaging with fans certainly costs money."

![A cartoon drawn by a reader and shared on Duke's official WeChat account](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607261421067fyEFrJeTKu0jIlV.jpg-w600)A cartoon drawn by a reader and shared on Duke's official WeChat account

### "Describe *The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry* as a bookstore on a beautiful little island, and it gets a first print run of 3,000. Describe it as getting through the hardest time of your life, and it can start at 100,000."

This year Duke is about to have its first foreign-licensed novel sell a million copies. *The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry* (《岛上书店》) came out in May and sold more than 500,000 copies in four months.

Hua Nan says this book was not played the same way as *Tibet Code*: "We call it a foreign-licensed emotional novel, which is the biggest segment of genre fiction in China. You have to distill the emotion and move people with a single sentence. That's how this market works. We can't sell the story. It takes hundreds of thousands of characters to tell a story well, and you can't make it interesting in a few dozen. What we do instead is distill the emotion." The slogan Duke distilled for *The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry*: "In everyone's life there is a hardest year, one that makes life beautiful and vast."

"Readers who see this line feel it themselves. They have been through a hard time, or are in one now. How do they get through that year, and how do they make a hard year beautiful and vast? That emotion moves people."

*The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry* could easily have been a niche literary book. It is strongly literary, its author is not Haruki Murakami or Gabriel García Márquez, and it has no hook like "Along the River During the Qingming Festival" or "Tibet." That is why its success surprised the publishing world all the more.

Hua Nan was not surprised: "Another publisher might introduce *The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry* as just a bookstore on a beautiful little island, and then you'd decide it could only start at 3,000 copies. But 'getting through the hardest time of your life' can start at 100,000."

Another Duke "foreign-licensed emotional novel," *Everything I Never Told You* (《无声告白》), is also on its way to becoming a super-bestseller. The book, by a Chinese-American woman writer, came out in August and sold more than 300,000 copies in just over a month. The "100,000-copy reason" Duke distilled for it: "All our lives, we are trying to shake off other people's expectations and find our true selves."

![Promotional poster for The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726142107ZBWU2dxqSrAHN9Ol.jpg-w600)

Promotional poster for *The Storied Life of A.J. Fikry*

![Cover of Everything I Never Told You](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726142108sDLCHjn12GylAaRi.jpg-w600)Cover of *Everything I Never Told You*

"A bookstore that wants to sell serious literature, books that sell 2,000 copies, has to sell Guo Jingming to survive."

Hua Nan says that a few days earlier he saw an article whose headline he agreed with: "It is because of films like *Tiny Times* that you can see *The Assassin* in ordinary cinemas. If *Tiny Times* hadn't heated up the film market, high-end art films would never have dreamed of getting into the cinema chains."

He thinks the book market works the same way: "Authors like Guo Jingming actually drive the whole market. You don't know this unless you run a business. A bookstore that wants to sell serious literature, books that sell 2,000 copies, has to sell Guo Jingming to survive."

Hua Nan once appeared at a forum with Guo Jingming and Bi Shumin: "The mood was, you know, whenever Guo Jingming is in the room, everyone gangs up on him. I said Guo Jingming works hard at what he does, and this market has room for him. Ms. Bi Shumin was sitting beside him, and I said, you keep doing your own work well, too. Readers will choose. There's no need to attack each other."

"A healthy market has to be varied, with every species in it and everyone leaving each other alone. If you hate me or can't stand me, that's fine."

![Guo Jingming at a book signing](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726142108sQC2zViLBRorjHb7.jpg-w600)

Guo Jingming at a book signing

"The market is getting more layered and richer. It used to be romance, mystery, foreign literature and a few business books. Now every kind of content can find its readers. The market is getting healthier and bigger."

Is the print market shrinking? Hua Nan says the claim simply doesn't hold up. The book market as a whole is growing: it dipped slightly in 2013, grew in 2014, and grew faster in 2015. Duke's sales were about 200 million yuan in both 2012 and 2013; now they are close to 400 million yuan. Hua Nan's own verdict, of course: "still not fast enough."

Duke publishes popular fiction, foreign-licensed books, children's books and more. It has *The Qingming Scroll Code* (《清明上河图密码》) for male readers, and romance queens such as Gu Man and Xia Qixi for teenage girls.

Hua Nan says Duke is about to launch a new imprint, provisionally called "Learning Wave": "A wave of learning is rising in China, and sales of serious books are growing, driven especially by businesspeople. Duke has published *Shi Yuzhu's Memoir*, *The House of Morgan* and *The Philosophy of Retail*, and the response beat our expectations. *The House of Morgan* is a very serious book, heavy and tiring to read, but its sales keep climbing. There's also *What Do Philosophers Do?*; the previous publisher botched it, and when we republished it the response was very good too. And we've seen other publishers make a success of books as serious as *Jerusalem: The Biography*."

As a merchant who makes his living selling printed books, Hua Nan is wholly optimistic. Reading, he believes, is a basic and permanent need, and on the whole the market is becoming richer and more layered.

"China's upper tier of people are reading more, and with more interest. One obvious sign: on planes, everyone in first and business class is holding a book. In China this learning wave runs from the top down. A few years ago, the people who read were two groups, middle and high school students and university students. Many young people stopped reading once they graduated. A super-bestseller used to have to be Guo Jingming or Gu Man. Now the reading habit has carried on and moved up the ladder. One reason is the example set by the people at the top; another is competitive pressure, because competition in society keeps getting fiercer."

"Look at CITIC Press's *Zero to One* this year, which reached a million copies. That's tied to the startup wave of the past few years. If you want to be a boss, you have to read not only business books but other things too, anthropology and sociology. The boss reads, so the executives read, and so do the people under them."

![Cover of The House of Morgan](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726142109EyNv7pcGh8ij2FQ4.jpg-w600)Cover of *The House of Morgan*

Online publishing actually offers fewer outlets than traditional print publishing. Qidian promotes only its top stars, and it has fewer display slots.

Hua Nan isn't afraid of web fiction. He treats it as a source of rights. A few years ago, when Duke went looking for authors, Tianya was the main source. Now it also works with Qidian and Jinjiang. Gu Man came out of Jinjiang.

Today Duke's sales split evenly between e-commerce and physical bookstores. Hua Nan believes traditional print publishing has particular advantages, and that online publishing in fact offers fewer outlets by comparison.

"Print publishing puts out several hundred thousand titles a year, and at least 100,000 of them get a chance to be displayed and sold. On Qidian everything seems to be hanging up there, but think about how much of it you've actually read. They only promote their big stars, and only the ones who cooperate fully, so overall their ability to make stars is much weaker than traditional publishing's. Their advantage in earlier years was a near-monopoly, so the stars they made were especially big. But they can't do what traditional publishing does, where authors selling 10,000, 50,000 or a million copies all make a decent living. And print actually has more million-selling superstars."

![Display slots in a bookstore](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607261421104FCfXA3eGWNBsPIK.jpg-w600)Display slots in a bookstore

The market is always restless. Its restlessness has nothing to do with you. Just don't be restless yourself. All you need is to see where you will be in the future.

Much of what happens in the market brings the word "restless" to mind: readers whose tastes bend whichever way the wind blows; publishers chasing trends and copying each other; "IP" that seemed to become fashionable overnight; licensing fees rising with the tide; and, as we noted at the start of this series, good books that so often fail to sell.

Hua Nan takes all this calmly: "Restlessness is permanent. The market is always restless. Now everyone talks about super IP and says the market is too restless. Are you going to complain about it? The market's restlessness has nothing to do with you. Just don't be restless yourself. All you need is to see where you will be in the future. You have to see past the restlessness. Actually there is no 'past' it. When this wave passes, the new market that takes shape will be just as restless. What you need to think about is where you want to stand in that next market."

"Now a lot of film screenwriters feel held down by novelists, and they complain: why should I have to adapt your lousy novel? Just because it's a super IP? People who talk like that are ignorant. If you're any good, turn the lousy novel into a good film, or build a film into a super IP out of nothing. You can take either path. Sitting there complaining that the market is restless and capital is heartless is just incompetence."

Hua Nan's logic: if you want to achieve something in the market, complaining is incompetence, and the only right response is to act. At first you may only scrape by, but if you are smart enough and capable enough, you will eventually find your place.

Looking back, Duke itself spent a while wandering the market without direction. At first Hua Nan and Wu You studied the American and Japanese book markets, the American one especially, and set out to publish romance novels. The books sold badly, and the company nearly went bankrupt. "After half a year we realized that American romance novels are read on the beach. China has no housewives and no middle class with that buying habit. In China romance novels are read by kids. In America they're read by housewives. It's different."

Only with *Bloody Official Career* (《流血的仕途》), the book that saved the company from bankruptcy (largely by luck, Hua Nan says), and then *Tibet Code*, did Duke gradually find its footing. "The biggest lesson is that you can't plan too much for yourself in this market. You take what you run into, then slowly re-plan."

So where will Duke be in the future? Hua Nan says: "There will be big changes, as the industries merge. Publishing used to be completely separate from film and games; now they are in fact one industry, and that will bring new ways of doing business."

Film and television adaptation is surely one of the most important directions: moving from the upstream of publishing into the much larger downstream, not just supplying content but taking part. Duke previously invested a few million yuan in the films *So Young* (《致我们终将逝去的青春》) and *Old Boys* (《老男孩》), and the returns were rich. In this year's contract with Alibaba for *The Qingming Scroll Code*, Duke also holds a 20% investment stake. It hopes to get more out of the book as well: stage plays, games, merchandise and so on.

![Still image related to Duke's film and adaptation projects](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726142110WJSyCu76VpGqmKgY.jpg-w600)

"Investing ourselves is inevitable, and directing ourselves is possible," Hua Nan sums up. What would he make? "An animated film."

Another field Duke is aiming at is comics and animation publishing, which will also lay the groundwork for film. On the walls of Hua Nan's office hang posters from Hollywood animation: the Minions, Baymax, Mike Wazowski. His desk is crowded with figures of Garfield, Snoopy, Spider-Man, Superman and more. Hua Nan has spent a lot of time studying them: "Character design is the ultimate thing in cultural brand management. Baymax wins the market entirely on its look. What it sells consumers is a warm, huggable image, something to project their feelings onto. Baymax is a single color, with the eyes and mouth stripped to the minimum. All of that is to make it instantly recognizable. In Chinese animation and film, the creators run things. The producer-led and director-led models both work for now, but they will fall behind. In the future it will certainly be brand managers who lead. We want to build an animation brand too, starting from a character."

![Buck-Toothed Imp, a character created by Duke Books](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702105012HjxFGIXivB3YhpeS.jpg-w600)"Buck-Toothed Imp," a character Duke once created, might have sold more than a million copies, but it was banned because its Chinese name contains the word "ghost"
